I am 48 years old and have only been back on the farm for two years after working in the city. With three people in my household and just 10.1 mu of land, I cannot afford to gamble. I follow what the veteran farmers in my village and the extension technician at the cooperative tell me. My cropping system is built around eggplant because that is where the money is—the wholesale buyers from Handan and Shijiazhuang come right to Quzhou for it. But I cannot put all my land into one crop in case prices crash or disease hits, so I keep my wheat and maize rotation for food security and household grain, and I grow chili on the side because it stores well and the spicy-variety buyers pay a good premium in autumn.

This year I will plant about 4.1 mu to eggplant, 3 mu to chili, and the remaining 3 mu to winter wheat followed by summer maize. I buy hybrid seeds for eggplant, chili, and maize—the seedling vendor at the county market guarantees the hybrids outperform the old seeds by 30 percent, and I saw that myself last year. For wheat, I use the improved "Jimai" variety the seed station subsidizes.

For fertilizer, I learned that vegetables are greedy. Eggplant needs heavy potassium or the fruits stay small and pale, so I will lay down compound fertilizer and top-dress twice. Wheat and maize get the standard N-P-K rates that the soil-test recommendation slip gave me: roughly 15–16 kg nitrogen per mu for the grains, and a bit more for the vegetables. 

Water is my advantage—I have a well. Eggplant cannot dry out in July and August, so I will irrigate every seven to ten days, about eight times through the season. Chili likes steady moisture but hates waterlogged roots, so six irrigations are enough. Wheat needs four critical waterings: before winter dormancy, at regreening, at jointing, and during grain filling. Summer maize is partly helped by the monsoon rains, but I will irrigate three times at key stages to be safe.

I do not like spending money on chemicals, but last year I lost eggplant leaves to aphids and chili to spider mites because I waited too long. This year I will spray eggplant six times and chili four times on a preventive schedule. Wheat usually needs only one fungicide spray, and maize needs two insecticide applications for armyworm and corn borer. 

For tillage, I plough deep for the wheat field in October to bury the stubble and break the plow pan. After the June wheat harvest, I rotary till quickly to plant maize before the summer planting window closes. The vegetable plots get rotary tilled to make fine raised beds for the transplanted seedlings.

My yield targets are conservative because I am still learning: 3,500 kg/mu for eggplant, 1,200 kg/mu for chili, 450 kg/mu for wheat, and 500 kg/mu for maize. If the weather holds and I manage the water right, these numbers should cover my costs and leave enough for my daughter's school fees.
